description_en: Known as "the Old Testament of music." A collection of preludes and fugues composed in all 24 major and minor keys. A monumental work exploring the possibilities of "well-tempered" tuning, which made every key usable.

Called the "Bible" of solo cello music. It draws rich harmony and contrapuntal melody from a single instrument, the cello. Each suite consists of a prelude and several dances (allemande, courante, sarabande, gigue and others).

The pinnacle of the solo violin repertoire. The "Chaconne" that closes Partita No. 2 in particular is regarded as one of the greatest violin works ever written as a single movement. The player must perform complex chords and counterpoint on just four strings.
A set of six concertos dedicated to the Margrave of Brandenburg. It is the supreme masterpiece of the concerto grosso style, in which varied groups of solo instruments contrast with the orchestra.

A vast oratorio (sacred dramatic music) on the Passion and death of Jesus, based on the Gospel of Matthew in the New Testament. It is regarded as the greatest work of sacred music in Western music history.

Famous for its overwhelming "Dum~ da-da-dum~" opening, it is the most popular of Bach's organ works. It combines a dramatic toccata section (improvisatory in style) with a tightly constructed fugue section.

Monteverdi's first opera, and the work regarded as the first great opera in music history. Based on the Greek myth of Orpheus, it portrays his journey to the underworld to win back his beloved wife, Euridice.

A monumental sacred work that Monteverdi composed in applying for the post of music director at St Mark's Basilica in Venice. It stands out for its grand scale, combining solo voices, chorus and orchestra, and for its dramatic expressiveness.

The most famous piece in Monteverdi's Eighth Book of Madrigals, Madrigali guerrieri et amorosi ("Madrigals of War and Love"). It dramatizes the grief of an abandoned nymph through the contrast between a solo voice (soprano) and a male trio. The lamenting melody over a repeating bass line (ground bass) is especially striking.

Monteverdi's last opera, in which his approach to operatic composition reached its peak. It deals with a historical episode that was radical for its time: the Roman emperor Nerone (Nero) and his lover Poppea commit all manner of wrongdoing for power, and she finally becomes empress. The duet "Pur ti miro, pur ti godo" ("I gaze at you, I delight in you") is famous.
Handel's greatest sacred work and the best-known oratorio in history. It covers the life of Jesus (birth, Passion, resurrection), and the "Hallelujah" chorus in Part 2 is the most famous number.
An orchestral suite composed for a royal boating party on the River Thames in England. The "Alla Hornpipe" movement is especially famous, and the work is marked by a brilliant, lively mood.

Composed for a large fireworks display celebrating the end of the War of the Austrian Succession. Its majestic Overture is famous, and the work was originally designed to be played solely by a large number of wind and percussion instruments.
An aria from Rinaldo, Handel's first opera to achieve great success in London. The heroine Almirena, taken captive, sings it as she laments her fate, and its sorrowful melody is very beautiful.
An aria sung by Serse (Xerxes), king of Persia, in admiration of the shade of a plane tree. Thanks to its peaceful, majestic melody, it is better known as "Handel's Largo."

A brilliant, majestic instrumental piece that opens Act 3 of the oratorio. It depicts the procession of the Queen of Sheba coming to visit King Solomon, and its festive character makes it a frequent choice at weddings and similar occasions.

The first of four anthems composed for the coronation of King George II of Great Britain. After the orchestra's majestic introduction, the chorus bursts in with an overwhelming effect. It has since become a tradition to perform it at the coronation of every British monarch. (It is also the work on which the UEFA Champions League anthem is based.)

The first four concertos from Vivaldi's collection of violin concertos Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione ("The Contest Between Harmony and Invention"), Op. 8. A masterpiece of program music, it depicts the scenery and feeling of each season based on sonnets (poems).
A collection of 12 concertos. It includes various concertos for one, two and four violins, and was the breakthrough work that spread Vivaldi's fame across Europe. Bach arranged six of them.
Vivaldi's most famous and most widely performed sacred vocal work. Composed for the choir and orchestra of the Pietà, a school for girls, it is a brilliant, festive piece in 12 movements.
One of the two mandolin concertos Vivaldi composed. A lovely piece that showcases the mandolin's clear, sparkling tremolo technique. The first movement is especially famous.
A piece in which two trumpets compete brilliantly in virtuosity, with the bright, grand sound of the baroque trumpet (natural trumpet) as its charm.

The sixth concerto in L'estro armonico (Op. 3), and one of Vivaldi's standard concertos, the one most frequently played by violin students. The vigorous rhythms of the first and third movements are striking.
Purcell's only through-composed opera and the supreme masterpiece of English opera. It portrays the tragic love between the Trojan hero Aeneas and Dido, queen of Carthage.

The lament near the end of Dido and Aeneas, sung by Queen Dido as she faces death after being abandoned by Aeneas. The harrowing yet beautiful melody unfolding over a chromatically descending ground bass is its greatest strength.

A "semi-opera" (dramatic music that includes spoken dialogue and play) adapted from Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream. Though it has no direct connection to the plot of the original, a masque combining lavish music, dance and stage machinery is inserted at the end of each act.

Solemn, mournful music composed for the funeral of Queen Mary II, who had been fond of him. It is striking for its majestic trumpet and trombone fanfares and its chorus, and, ironically, it was also performed at Purcell's own funeral a few months later.

Incidental music for the play of the same name. Its "Rondeau" movement became even more famous when the 20th-century composer Benjamin Britten used it as the theme of The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra.
Known by the nickname "Cortège" (procession) or "Promenade." It is characterized by a solemn, bright theme reminiscent of a fanfare, and seems to depict a splendid march at the Spanish court.
Famous under the nickname "La Caccia" (The Hunt), it is characterized by a cheerful, rhythmic theme that seems to imitate hunting horn calls. It is one of the most popular of Scarlatti's sonatas.

One of Scarlatti's best-known sonatas, creating a dreamy, meditative atmosphere. Its cross-hand technique, in which the hands cross over each other, is prominent, and it evokes the resonance of the Spanish guitar.

A piece characterized by fierce tremolo (rapid repeated notes) and arpeggios that seem to imitate the "rasgueado" strumming technique of the Spanish guitar. It demands extreme virtuosity and is popular with pianists as a challenging piece of repertoire.
Together with Kk. 27, it is counted among Scarlatti's most lyrical and introspective sonatas. It is marked by a plaintive, beautiful melody and even hints at Romantic sensibility.
A sonata often called by the nickname "Pastorale." It is marked by a lyrical, peaceful melody, and is popular as one of Scarlatti's relatively accessible yet beautiful sonatas.

Number 1 in the Kirkpatrick catalogue and the first piece in the first collection of sonata exercises that Scarlatti published in 1738 (Essercizi per Gravicembalo). An elegant, well-ordered piece showing his early style.
Rameau's most famous opéra-ballet. It strings together four different "exotic" stories (Turkey, Peru, Persia, America) in an omnibus format. The "Danse des Sauvages" in Act 4 is especially famous.

A piece from his second book of harpsichord pieces (1724). A lively, light dance that imitates the rhythm of the tambourin, a small Provençal drum. It is one of the best-known works among Rameau's keyboard pieces.

The closing piece of the A minor suite in the Nouvelles suites de pièces de clavecin ("New Suites of Harpsichord Pieces"), published around 1728. It consists of an elegant gavotte theme followed by six brilliant, virtuosic variations (doubles).

A piece in the G major suite of the Nouvelles suites de pièces de clavecin. A masterpiece of the "character piece" (descriptive miniature), it depicts the clucking and movements of a hen on the keyboard in a playful, finely crafted way.

Rameau's representative tragédie en musique (lyric tragedy), counted among the greatest of his operas. It deals with the brotherly affection and love of the twin brothers Castor (a mortal) and Pollux (an immortal).

Rameau's shocking first opera, presented when he was 50. It is based on Racine's tragedy Phèdre. To audiences accustomed to the music of Lully, Rameau's bold harmony and orchestration came as a shock, and this controversial masterpiece set off the "Lullistes versus Ramistes" dispute.

The title means "table music." A large collection of instrumental music published by Telemann, it is organized into three "Productions," each containing an overture, a concerto, a quartet, a trio, a solo sonata and more, like a variety gift set.

Regarded as one of the very first full-fledged solo viola concertos in history, and a very important work. It makes good use of the viola's warm, elegant tone and is now core repertoire for every viola major.
A concerto-like suite for alto recorder (or flute). It consists of a French overture and various dances, and the final "Air à l'Italien" movement and the "Polonoise" are especially famous.
A programmatic suite for string ensemble depicting scenes from Cervantes's novel Don Quixote. Witty depictions such as "The Fight with the Windmills" and "Sancho's Donkey" stand out.

A set of 12 quartets that Telemann composed around his visit to Paris in the 1730s. Scored for flute, violin, viola da gamba (or cello) and harpsichord, they are counted as masterpieces of chamber music in which French and Italian styles are exquisitely blended.

Corelli's most famous work, the eighth of the 12 concerti grossi in his Op. 6 collection. It bears a note that it was composed for Christmas night, and the peaceful, beautiful melody of the final movement, the "Pastorale," is especially famous.

The last of the 12 sonatas in Corelli's Op. 5 collection of violin sonatas. It consists of 23 brilliant variations on the melody of "La Folia," a dance tune popular at the time. It is the work in which Corelli's violin technique reaches its peak, and is regarded as the most representative example of "La Folia" variations.

Corelli's last collection, the culmination of his career. It shows the peak of the concerto grosso style, in which a small group of two violins and cello (the concertino) contrasts with the full orchestra (ripieno, or tutti). The "Christmas Concerto" is included.

The most famous of Corelli's trio sonata collections. Scored for two violins, cello and organ (basso continuo). A model of the "sonata da chiesa" (church sonata), it established the four-movement layout (slow-fast-slow-fast) and is marked by a serious, solemn mood.

The most important and best-known work in which Gluck's "opera reform" was first applied. It eliminates the needless displays of virtuosity of traditional opera seria (da capo arias) and is composed so that the music serves the drama. It deals with the Greek myth of Orpheus.

A famous ballet piece from Act 2 of the opera above. It depicts the dance of the spirits when Orfeo arrives in Elysium, the paradise. The clear, beautiful flute melody is so famous that the piece is often performed on its own.

In Act 3 of the opera above, a despairing aria sung by Orfeo, who loses his wife Euridice a second time after breaking the taboo by looking back at her. It is famous for a tragic and beautiful melody that concentrates Gluck's "noble simplicity."

Gluck's second reform opera, following Orfeo. It deals with the noble sacrifice of Queen Alceste, who resolves to die in place of her husband, King Admetus. The preface to this opera is very famous as a manifesto setting out Gluck's ideals of "opera reform."
Regarded as the greatest masterpiece among Gluck's reform operas. Composed in Paris and based on Greek tragedy, it achieves dramatic tension and musical unity close to perfection.
One of Mozart's best-known instrumental works. The title means "a little serenade," and it is characterized by a light, elegant melody. The first movement is especially famous.
One of Mozart's three great symphonies, famous for the tragic yet passionate theme of its first movement. A masterpiece that hints at Romantic sensibility.
Mozart's last symphony. The pinnacle of the classical symphony, it is most remarkable for the brilliant, majestic fugal writing in the fourth and final movement.

A comic opera (opera buffa) of genius, ahead of its time. It cheerfully portrays the wit of the servant Figaro, who stands up to the privileges of the nobility (the "right of the first night"). From the famous overture on, every aria is counted a masterpiece.
Mozart's last opera, completed shortly before his death. A German-language Singspiel, it is a fairy-tale-like, philosophical work embodying Freemason ideas. The "Queen of the Night aria" is famous.

Mozart's unfinished posthumous work. A requiem mass commissioned by an unidentified patron, it is said by legend that he composed it with a premonition of his own death. His pupil Süssmayr completed it.
One of Mozart's most dramatic and Romantic piano concertos. Beethoven was especially fond of it and even composed cadenzas for it himself.
The third movement, the "Rondo alla Turca" (Turkish-style rondo), is so famous that the sonata is known by the nickname "Turkish March." It is also popular with piano students.
The last concerto Mozart completed. A masterpiece that expresses the beauty of the clarinet to the utmost, it is known especially for its second-movement Adagio.
The best-known symphony in Western music history, opening with the famous "Da-da-da-DUM~" motif. It shows in compressed form Beethoven's musical world of "through suffering to joy."
Beethoven's last symphony. A revolutionary work that was the first to bring a vocal chorus (Schiller's "Ode to Joy") into its fourth movement. It carries a message of humanity and harmony.

Famous for the anecdote that Beethoven originally intended to dedicate it to Napoleon but, enraged when Napoleon proclaimed himself emperor, tore up the dedication. A work of vast scale that broke the framework of the classical symphony.
Beethoven's best-known piano sonata. The dreamy first movement is especially famous, and the nickname "Moonlight" was given after Beethoven's death by the poet Rellstab.
A masterpiece among Beethoven's early sonatas. It won great popularity for its tragic yet majestic introduction to the first movement and its passionate melodies.
Beethoven's last piano concerto. Characterized by a grand scale on a par with a symphony and brilliant piano virtuosity, it shows a majesty fitting its nickname, "Emperor."
Beethoven's only violin concerto. Together with the concertos of Mendelssohn and Brahms, it is counted among the three great violin concertos, and has a grand, noble beauty.
The most famous piano piece in the world among the bagatelles (short pieces) Beethoven left behind. Who "Elise" was remains a matter of debate.
One of Haydn's "London" symphonies. Famous for the anecdote that, in the quietly played second movement, a sudden loud chord (timpani and all the instruments) bursts out to startle the audience.
In the second movement, the bassoon and strings rhythmically depict the "tick-tock" of a clock pendulum, which earned the symphony the nickname "The Clock."

A witty piece Haydn composed for the musicians who had not been granted leave. It is famous for the performance in the fourth and final movement in which the players put out their candles one by one and leave the stage.
The second movement is a set of variations on the melody Haydn composed as the Austrian national anthem (the "Emperor's Hymn"). The melody later became that of the German national anthem.
One of Haydn's greatest masterpieces. Composed after he was deeply impressed by Handel's Messiah, it depicts the seven days of creation in the Old Testament in grand and vivid fashion.
The first great concerto composed for the newly invented keyed trumpet. It shows both the brilliant virtuosity and the lyricism of the trumpet, and is standard repertoire for trumpeters.

It began as a collaboration with Gluck, but Salieri completed it when Gluck's health declined. It was a great success in Paris and earned Salieri recognition as the successor to Gluck's "opera reform."

Composed to a libretto by Beaumarchais (author of the original play The Marriage of Figaro), it is one of Salieri's most ambitious operas. It was a great success in Paris just before the French Revolution.
A comic opera based on Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor. (It is a different work from the opera of the same name later composed by Verdi.)
Salieri's best-known and liveliest symphony. It shows his side as an instrumental composer.
A collection of études known in Korea as "Czerny 30." It consists of essential études for completing basic piano technique.
Called "Czerny 40" in Korea. A collection of 40 études for training speed (velocity) and technique at a higher level than Czerny 30.
Called "Czerny 50" in Korea. An advanced collection of études that gathers nearly every kind of brilliant technique a pianist needs.
Called "Czerny 100" in Korea, it is one of the first collections of études that beginning pianists encounter.
A witty symphony in which toy instruments such as the cuckoo, trumpet and drum play along with the orchestra. (For a long time it was mistakenly attributed to Haydn.)
A trumpet concerto showing the transitional style between the Baroque and the Classical. The slow melody of the second movement is famous.
A concerto that features the alto trombone, uncommon at the time, as its solo instrument. Today it is important repertoire for trombonists.
The most famous piece among all of Boccherini's works. Because of its elegant, lyrical melody, it has been widely used in films and commercials.
The most famous of Boccherini's cello concertos. (However, what is played today is often the version arranged by the 19th-century cellist Grützmacher.)
A lively chamber work composed by Boccherini, who worked at the Spanish court, using the rhythm of the Spanish dance, the fandango.
C.P.E. Bach's best-known short piece for piano (clavier). A technical étude in which the two hands cross rapidly while playing arpeggios.
A concerto that shows well the sharp contrasts of intense emotion characteristic of the Empfindsamer Stil (the "sensitive style"). Baroque rhythmic drive and Classical drama coexist.
C.P.E. Bach's representative flute concerto. Although the influence of his father, J.S. Bach, can be felt, the Sturm und Drang-like intensity stands out.
A representative vocal work that carries on J.S. Bach's majestic sacred music while adding Classical clarity and dramatic expression.
A symphony in the elegant, light galant style, worthy of "the London Bach." It is also known as the overture to Mozart's opera Lucio Silla.
A sinfonia concertante in which two violins and a cello blend with the orchestra. The young Mozart was influenced by this genre.
Long known as a work by J.C. Bach and widely performed, it was revealed to be a forgery by the 20th-century French cellist Henri Casadesus. Even so, it remains a popular piece of viola repertoire.
One of the first great concertos for the clarinet. It displays the clarinet's virtuosity and lyricism brilliantly, and clearly shows the style of the Mannheim school.
A masterpiece among early symphonies, clearly showing the "Mannheim crescendo" (a gradually growing sound) and the "Mannheim rocket" (a rising arpeggio), hallmarks of Stamitz and the Mannheim school.
A trumpet concerto composed before Haydn's. Although Baroque influence remains, the lively Classical energy stands out.
Study material that piano students around the world work through before Czerny. These are the most widely used pieces for learning Classical formal beauty and basic piano technique.
A collection of 100 études whose title means "Steps to Parnassus (the heaven of music)." A textbook of modern piano technique, it was even parodied by Debussy.
Clementi's most dramatic and Romantic sonata. A programmatic work depicting the tragedy of the abandoned Dido in Virgil's epic poem.

A song cycle of 24 songs that Schubert composed shortly before his death. It portrays the despair of a young man who, having failed in love, wanders through a snowstorm, and is the summit of German song.

A song of genius that Schubert composed at the age of 18. Based on a poem by Goethe, it has a single singer act four voices (the narrator, the father, the son and the Erlking), while the piano depicts the sound of galloping hooves.

A chamber work that uses the melody of his own song "Die Forelle" ("The Trout") as the theme of a set of variations in the fourth movement. The scoring of piano and string quartet is unusual (a double bass is included), and the mood is bright and cheerful.
Schubert's best-known symphony. Although only two movements were completed, it is regarded as a perfect masterpiece in itself. It announced the beginning of the Romantic symphony.

It uses the melody of his own song "Death and the Maiden" as the theme of the variations in the second movement. A masterpiece showing the most dramatic and intense tragic beauty among Schubert's chamber music.
The best-known collection of Schubert's short piano pieces. It consists of four pieces and is especially famous for the lyrical melody of No. 3 in G♭ major.

Together with the concertos of Beethoven and Brahms, it is counted among the three great Romantic violin concertos. Its innovative structure has the solo violin play the theme right at the start of the first movement.
Music for Shakespeare's comedy. It consists of the overture (Op. 21) composed at age 17 and the incidental music (Op. 61) added later. The "Wedding March" in particular is world-famous.

A symphony composed with inspiration from Mendelssohn's travels in Italy. The first movement, which evokes dazzling sunshine and blue skies, and the fiery fourth movement, a "saltarello" (an Italian dance), are famous.

A collection of piano pieces whose title means "songs without words." Made up of eight books (Opp. 19b, 30, 38, 53, 62, 67, 85, 102), it includes the well-known "Spring Song" and "Venetian Gondola Song."

A concert overture composed during a trip to the Hebrides islands of Scotland, inspired by Fingal's Cave, where the waves crash. A masterpiece of program music, outstanding in its depiction of scenery.
Famous for the anecdote that Chopin composed it in a fury on hearing that his homeland, Poland, had been occupied by Russia. It is characterized by fierce arpeggios in the left hand.
One of the most popular of Chopin's piano pieces. The fierce opening and closing sections contrast dramatically with the middle section, which stands out for its sweet lyricism.
The first work in which Chopin elevated the "ballade" genre into a piano solo piece. With its epic, dramatic development, it is counted among Chopin's greatest masterpieces.
A work that expands the polonaise, a Polish folk dance, to a majestic, heroic symphonic scale. It shows Chopin's patriotism and spirit.
The best-known of Chopin's nocturnes. Characterized by a sweet, lyrical melody, it has been used in numerous films and dramas.
Composed just before Chopin left his homeland, Poland. The orchestra is judged somewhat thin, but the poetic beauty and brilliance of the piano part are overwhelming.
The anecdote goes that Chopin composed it after watching his dog chase its own tail. It is also called the "Minute" Waltz, but it is very difficult to play in under a minute.
A representative song cycle composed in 1840, Schumann's "year of song," when he married Clara. Based on poems by Heine, it portrays the joy and anguish of love and the pain of heartbreak.
A suite of 13 short piano pieces written in remembrance of childhood. It is a work for adults. No. 7, "Träumerei" (Dreaming), is very famous.
A masterpiece of the Romantic piano concerto. The orchestra and piano fuse as closely as in a symphony, and Schumann's passion and lyricism are in harmony.
A symphony Schumann composed with inspiration from the scenery of the Rhine and the grandeur of Cologne Cathedral. Its five-movement structure is unusual, and it is full of Romantic vitality.

A suite of 21 character pieces depicting in music the figures at a masked ball (carnival), such as Pierrot and Harlequin, as well as Schumann's own inner selves (Florestan and Eusebius), Chopin, Paganini and others.
One of Liszt's most beloved piano pieces, ranking alongside Chopin's nocturnes in popularity. Originally composed as a song and arranged for solo piano, it is characterized by its sweet melody.

A piano étude based on the theme of "La Campanella" ("The Bell"), the third movement of Paganini's Violin Concerto No. 2. It is characterized by brilliant high-register technique that imitates the sound of bells.

The most famous of Liszt's 19 Hungarian Rhapsodies. The contrast between the improvisatory opening of Gypsy (Romani) music (the lassan) and the fiercely accelerating second half (the friska) is striking.

The representative work of the "symphonic poem" genre that Liszt created. Based on Lamartine's poem that sees life as a prelude to death, it depicts various facets of life (love, struggle, triumph and more).
One of the 12 études that show Liszt's superhuman technique. A fierce, heroic piece depicting the hero Mazeppa as he gallops across the wilderness tied to a horse.
The opening of Act 3 of Die Walküre, the second opera of the four-part Ring of the Nibelung cycle. It gained overwhelming recognition after its use in the film Apocalypse Now.

A revolutionary opera that changed the course of Western music history. Through an ambiguous harmony known as the "Tristan chord," it expresses the longing of unresolved love and heralded the breakdown of tonality.
The "wedding march" from Act 3, which, along with Mendelssohn's wedding march, is the piece most used at wedding ceremonies around the world today.
A masterpiece among Wagner's early Romantic operas. A brilliant overture in which the devout theme represented by the "Pilgrims' Chorus" contrasts with the sensual theme of the "Venusberg."

Verdi's most famous and beloved opera. It portrays the tragic love between Violetta, a woman of Parisian society, and the naive young Alfredo. The Brindisi (Drinking Song) and other numbers are famous.
One of the three great masterpieces of Verdi's middle period. It portrays the tragedy of the hunchbacked jester Rigoletto. The aria "La donna è mobile" is world-famous.

A spectacular opera composed to commemorate the opening of the Suez Canal. Set in ancient Egypt, it portrays the tragic love between Aida, princess of the enemy nation Ethiopia, and the Egyptian general Radamès. The "Triumphal March" is famous.

A chorus sung by Hebrew slaves taken captive in Babylon as they long for their homeland. Called a "second national anthem" by Italians, who were then under Austrian rule, it made Verdi a national hero.

A requiem mass that Verdi composed in memory of the great writer Manzoni, whom he revered. Although it is sacred music, it is characterized by "operatic" fierce drama and emotional expression, and the "Dies Irae" section is especially overwhelming.

Brahms's first symphony, which he labored over for more than 20 years. It inherits the "struggle and triumph" design, from C minor to C major, that resembles Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, and was praised as "Beethoven's Tenth Symphony."
Brahms's most lyrical and Romantic symphony. The wistful melody of the third movement, "Poco allegretto," is very famous and is often used in films and dramas.
The best-known of Brahms's 21 Hungarian Dances (originally for piano four hands). It is characterized by fierce Gypsy-style rhythms and a wistful melody.
Together with Beethoven's concerto, it is counted as one of the two great peaks of the Romantic violin concerto. It is characterized by a symphonic, grand scale and a masculine breadth.
Not the traditional Latin requiem (mass for the dead), but a requiem "to comfort the living," set to German texts that Brahms himself selected from the Luther Bible.
Tchaikovsky's last symphony and his greatest masterpiece. Its radical structure ends not with the traditional "joyful" finale but with an utterly despairing, sorrowful Adagio (slow movement).
The most famous of the Romantic piano concertos. The melody of its grand, brilliant opening is so well known that nearly everyone has heard it at least once.

Together with the concertos of Beethoven, Mendelssohn and Brahms, it is counted among the four great Romantic violin concertos. It is characterized by wistful, distinctively Russian melodies and brilliant virtuosity.
One of Tchaikovsky's three great ballets, a fairy-tale work set at Christmas. The suite, including the "Waltz of the Flowers" and the "Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy," is especially famous.

The first of Tchaikovsky's three great ballets and a byword for classical ballet. It tells the story of Princess Odette, who has been cursed and turned into a swan. The theme melody of the "Scene" is famous.
Program music composed to commemorate the failure of Napoleon's Russian campaign. It is famous for its grand finale, which uses real cannon fire and bells.
A collection of études for solo violin, called the "New Testament of the violin." It gathers every technique the violin can express. The last one, No. 24 in A minor, is the most famous.

The third-movement rondo, "La Campanella" ("The Bell"), is especially famous. It is characterized by brilliant violin flageolet (harmonics) technique imitating the sound of bells, and Liszt arranged it as a piano piece.
The most widely performed of Paganini's concertos. It combines brilliant violin virtuosity with aria-like melodies in the style of Italian opera.
Rossini's greatest masterpiece, a comic opera (opera buffa). It portrays the exploits of the witty barber Figaro. The aria "Largo al factotum" ("I am the city's jack-of-all-trades") is famous.
The overture to Rossini's last opera, William Tell. It is divided into four parts, and the last, the "March of the Swiss Soldiers" (with its lively galloping hooves), is very famous.
One of Rossini's famous opera overtures, it opens with the distinctive rhythm of the snare drum.

Berlioz's breakthrough work and a masterpiece of program music. It depicts five visions dreamed by a jilted artist under the influence of opium. The "idée fixe," symbolizing the beloved woman, appears in every movement.
An operatic legend (dramatic cantata) based on Goethe's Faust. The "Hungarian March" (Rákóczi March) from it became famous for its brilliant orchestration and is often performed on its own.
A brilliant concert overture composed from melodies of his own opera Benvenuto Cellini. It depicts the frenzied atmosphere of the Roman carnival.
The overture to Glinka's second opera. Full of the racing rhythms and lively energy typical of Russian music, it is a regular in orchestral repertoire.
The first Russian national opera. Its patriotic story is that the Russian peasant Ivan Susanin sacrifices himself to save the Tsar from Polish troops.
Glinka's best-known song. A beautiful melody depicting the trilling of a skylark, it became even more famous when Balakirev arranged it as a piano solo.
Counted as the greatest of Clara Schumann's chamber works. Although the influence of her husband Robert Schumann can be seen, her own lyricism and solid sense of structure stand out.
An ambitious work she completed at the age of 16. It shows both the Romantic virtuoso side she shared with her contemporary Chopin and a deep lyricism.
A late work, composed for the violinist Joachim, her close friend. Deep, intimate Romantic sensibility stands out.
Franck's best-known and most beloved chamber work. It was composed as a wedding present for the violinist Eugène Ysaÿe. The four movements are organically linked by a single theme (cyclic form).
The representative French symphony of the late 19th century. A masterpiece characterized by Wagnerian chromatic harmony, organ-like grandeur and "cyclic form."
Originally part of the Mass for three voices (Op. 12), it became widely known when arranged as a solo piece titled "Bread of Life." It is characterized by a devout, beautiful melody.
The most popular of Bruckner's symphonies. It has the character of program music depicting a medieval forest, castle and knights, and the horn solo in the first movement is famous.
The symphony that first brought Bruckner great success. The second-movement Adagio is solemn, mournful music written in memory of Wagner, whom he revered, upon his death.
The most famous of Bruckner's a cappella (unaccompanied choral) motets. Composed for the dedication of Linz Cathedral, it stands out for its mysterious, devout harmony.
A waltz that is something like a "second national anthem," symbolizing Vienna, Austria. It is a regular encore at the Vienna New Year's Concert and the most famous waltz in the world.
The overture to Die Fledermaus, the most successful operetta (comic opera) by Strauss, the "Waltz King." It concentrates the cheerful, lively melodies featured in the operetta.
A fast, fierce polka depicting thunder (timpani) and lightning (cymbals). A regular in the repertoire of the Vienna New Year's Concert.
Together with By the Beautiful Blue Danube, it is counted as the essence of the Viennese waltz. The scenery of the Vienna Woods and the solo for the folk instrument zither are striking.
A piano suite depicting 10 pictures in music, written after seeing an exhibition of works left by his friend, the painter Hartmann, who died young. The theme called "Promenade" links the pictures.

A version of Mussorgsky's original piano suite arranged with brilliant flair by Ravel, the "magician of the orchestra." Today it is performed more often than the original, and the final piece, "The Great Gate of Kiev," is especially overwhelming.
A piece depicting witches and demons gathering on Bald Mountain on St. John's Eve for a frenzied revel. The version arranged by Rimsky-Korsakov is famous.

The supreme masterpiece of Russian national opera. It realistically portrays the guilt and downfall of Boris Godunov, who took the throne after murdering the tsar, as well as the suffering of the Russian people.

One of the most popular works in the history of Western opera. It portrays the free-spirited love and tragic death of the Gypsy woman Carmen. All the arias, including the "Habanera" and the "Toreador Song," are famous.

Incidental music composed for Alphonse Daudet's play L'Arlésienne ("The Girl from Arles"). The play failed, but the music became very popular and was arranged into two orchestral suites. The "Farandole" and "Minuet" are famous.
A duet for tenor and baritone from Bizet's early opera The Pearl Fishers (WD 13). It is famous for a beautiful melody that sings of the friendship of two men who love the same woman.
A symphony Bizet composed as a 17-year-old student. A Classical-style work influenced by Haydn and Mozart, it is characterized by bright, witty energy.

Dvořák's greatest masterpiece, composed in New York in the United States. Inspired by African American spirituals and Native American music, it is known for the Largo melody of the second movement ("Goin' Home").
Counted as the greatest masterpiece among cello concertos of the Romantic era. It combines cello virtuosity, deep lyricism and symphonic grandeur.
The work that brought Dvořák international fame. A collection of lively, colorful orchestral pieces based on folk dances of Bohemia, in the Czech lands.
Chamber music composed in the United States at the same time as the New World Symphony. It is characterized by pentatonic melodies in the style of African American spirituals and exotic rhythms.
The seventh of the eight Humoresques (Op. 101), and the most famous and best-loved melody among all of Dvořák's short pieces.
A symphonic suite based on the Arabian Nights, depicting Scheherazade (solo violin) telling stories to the Sultan. It shows brilliant orchestration at its height.
An intermezzo from Act 3 of the opera. It is famous for its breathlessly fast passages depicting the prince, transformed into a bumblebee, flying away.
A five-movement orchestral piece composed on Spanish folk melodies and rhythms. Dazzling orchestration and the brilliant virtuosity of the solo instruments stand out.
A majestic, brilliant concert overture composed on the atmosphere of the Russian Orthodox Easter festival and its chants.
Unlike the traditional requiem, it omits the "Dies Irae" and portrays death as peaceful rest. The fourth movement, "Pie Jesu," in particular is famous.
An orchestral piece based on the pavane, a slow, elegant old Spanish court dance. It is much loved for its dreamy, sweet melody.
Originally incorporated into the Pelléas et Mélisande suite, it is characterized by a melody in the style of a pastoral Sicilian dance. It is often played as a flute or cello solo.
The best-known of Fauré's many songs (mélodies). A lyrical work singing of the joy of being reunited with a lover in a dream and the sadness after waking.

One of Puccini's biggest successes. It portrays the heartbreaking love story of poor artists (Mimì and Rodolfo) in the back streets of Paris. "Che gelida manina" ("Your tiny hand is frozen") and "Mi chiamano Mimì" ("My name is Mimì") are famous.

An aria from Puccini's unfinished final work, Turandot. It is the song of victory sung by Prince Calaf after he solves the princess's riddles, and the "Vincerò" ("I will win!") passage is overwhelming.

An opera about the tragedy of the singer Tosca, her lover Cavaradossi, and Scarpia, the chief of police who leads them to ruin. "E lucevan le stelle" ("And the stars were shining") and "Vissi d'arte" ("I lived for art, I lived for love") are famous.
Set in Nagasaki, Japan, it portrays the tragic love of the geisha Cio-Cio-San, abandoned by the American naval officer Pinkerton. "Un bel dì" ("One fine day") is famous.
An aria from Puccini's only comic opera, Gianni Schicchi. It is the song of the daughter Lauretta, who pleads with her father to let her marry the man she loves.
One of Mahler's most popular symphonies. Vast in scale, it deals with the philosophical theme of "death and resurrection," and a chorus enters in the fifth movement.
A symphony that begins with a funeral-march-like first movement and ends with a jubilant finale. The fourth-movement "Adagietto," played by strings and harp alone, is especially famous.
Mahler's first symphony, composed in his twenties. An ambitious work of the young Mahler that blends sounds of nature, folk-like melodies, a funeral march and more.

Called the "Symphony of a Thousand" because a performance requires nearly 1,000 people (a large orchestra, eight vocal soloists and three choruses). It carries the most affirmative message among Mahler's works.

A "song symphony" in six movements based on Chinese poems, including those of Li Bai (Li Taibai). Because of the superstition of the "curse of the Ninth," Mahler did not call it his "Symphony No. 9." It is one of Mahler's most pessimistic and profound masterpieces.
The third of the four pieces in the Suite bergamasque. The most famous of all Debussy's piano pieces, it is a dreamy, beautiful work often used as a byword for "Impressionist" music.
A symphonic poem based on Mallarmé's Symbolist poem, depicting the dream of a faun on a languid afternoon. A monumental work that announced the beginning of "Impressionist music."
Debussy's greatest orchestral masterpiece, depicting the ever-changing scenery and colors of the sea across three movements (including "From Dawn to Noon on the Sea").
A suite of six short piano pieces composed for his daughter Emma. The "Golliwogg's Cakewalk" movement is famous, and it playfully quotes Wagner's "Tristan chord."
The first of the two Arabesques (L. 66). A short piano piece characterized by the elegant, lyrical melody of Debussy's early style.
Rachmaninoff's greatest masterpiece and a byword for the Romantic piano concerto. It is loved around the world for its deep melancholy, explosive passion and sweet melodies.
One of the concertos reputed to be the most difficult, demanding extreme technique and stamina from the pianist. It also became widely known to the public through the film Shine.
A set of variations for piano and orchestra on the theme of Paganini's Caprice No. 24. Variation 18 (a melody made by inverting the theme) is especially famous.
The last of the 14 songs of Op. 34. A sad and beautiful melody sung without words, on a vowel ("ah") alone, it is performed in arrangements for many different instruments.
A short piano piece composed at age 23 that brought him worldwide fame. It is characterized by solemn, dark chords reminiscent of the bells of the Kremlin.
Ravel's best-known experimental orchestral work, in which a single rhythm and two melodies repeat for 15 minutes with changing instrumentation, ending in a grand finale.
A piano piece (later orchestrated) written while imagining a dance that a young infanta (princess) might have danced at the old Spanish court. It is much loved for its antique, elegant melody.
A piano piece depicting water spurting and glittering. An innovative work that, by taking "water" as its subject before Debussy, announced the beginning of Impressionist piano technique.
A light, witty concerto composed under the influence of the jazz Ravel encountered on his trip to the United States. The beautiful piano solo of the second-movement Adagio is famous.
Ravel's largest and most brilliant ballet music. Suite No. 2 ("Daybreak," "Pantomime," "General Dance") shows the essence of his orchestration.

The overture to Der Freischütz, which opened the era of German Romantic opera. It condenses the opera's key themes: the mystery of the forest, the sinister presence of the devil, and the joy of victory.
A piano piece depicting a scene at a ball in which a gentleman invites a lady to dance and they waltz together. It became the origin of the Romantic "waltz."
A concerto that maximizes the dark tone of the clarinet and its brilliant technique. Together with Mozart's concerto, it is important repertoire for clarinetists.
Johann Strauss I's most famous work. It closes the Vienna New Year's Concert and is known for the tradition of the audience clapping along with the beat.
Together with his son's (Strauss II's) By the Beautiful Blue Danube, it is regarded as the most lyrical and beautiful of the father's waltzes.

One of the greatest masterpieces of Romantic ballet (the "ballet blanc"). It portrays the tragedy of Giselle, an innocent country girl who dies through the betrayal of a nobleman and becomes a ghost (a Wili).
One of the most widely sung Christmas carols in the world. It is better known by the title "O Holy Night."
An arrangement in which Gounod set a melody to a Latin prayer text over the harmony of the Prelude No. 1 in C major from Book 1 of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier.
Gounod's signature work. Based on Goethe's Faust, it deals with the story of Faust, who makes a contract with the devil Mephistopheles, pledging his soul.
A five-act opera based on Shakespeare's tragedy of the same name. Four love duets and the aria "Juliet's Waltz" are famous.
Offenbach's most famous operetta (comic opera). It satirizes Greek myth, and it won immortal fame through the "Can-can" dance music at the end of the overture.
Offenbach's only grand opera and his last work. The duet in Act 3, the "Barcarolle," is famous for its dreamy, beautiful melody.

The second of the six symphonic poems of Má Vlast ("My Country"), which depict the history and nature of the Czech lands. Depicting the flow of the Vltava (Moldau), the lifeline of the Czech lands, it is Smetana's most famous piece.
A representative work of Czech national opera. It portrays a love story between country folk with cheerful dance music. The overture in particular is famous for its racing, fast string passages.
Ballet music from Act 2 of Borodin's unfinished opera Prince Igor. Its exotic, fierce rhythms and enchanting melodies make it a frequent concert piece on its own.
An exotic symphonic poem set on the vast steppes of Central Asia, depicting the meeting of Russian and Eastern melodies.
Borodin's representative symphony, full of vigorous energy reminiscent of Russian heroic epics.
An orchestral suite in 14 movements that cheerfully depicts various animals such as the lion, the swan, the aquarium and the kangaroo. The "Swan" movement is especially famous.
A symphonic poem depicting the legend of skeletons rising from their graves to dance to the playing of Death's violin. The xylophone depicts the sound of bones clattering.
Saint-Saëns's last symphony. A masterpiece that combines an organ and two pianos with the orchestra to create a majestic, brilliant sound.
An aria from Act 2 of the biblical opera Samson and Delilah, which Delilah sings to seduce Samson. It is a captivating, sensual aria.
